source_batch.unit_label: Module A unit 3: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion, Skewness, Kurtosis

facts.statement: Measures of central tendency (averages) condense data into a single value and make comparison between data sets possible. A good measure is rigidly defined, simple to understand and calculate, based on all the observations, capable of further mathematical treatment, least affected by sampling fluctuations, not unduly affected by extreme values and easy to interpret. The three kinds of average are the mean (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic), the median and the mode.

The arithmetic mean of raw data is the sum of the observations divided by their number; for grouped data it is the sum of frequency times value divided by the total frequency, using class marks for class intervals. The combined mean of two groups of sizes n1 and n2 with means m1 and m2 is (n1 m1 + n2 m2) / (n1 + n2), extended in the same way to more groups. A mean found to include a wrong observation is corrected by taking the original sum (n times the mean), subtracting the wrong value and adding the right one, then dividing by n. A missing value or frequency is found by writing the mean equation and solving it.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 48-50, sections 3.2 and 3.3 and Examples 1 to 9

facts.statement: The arithmetic mean is rigidly defined, simple, based on all observations, readily treated algebraically and least affected by sampling fluctuations. Its demerits are that it is highly affected by extreme values, cannot properly average ratios and percentages, is not appropriate for a highly skewed distribution, cannot be computed accurately if an item is missing, may not coincide with any observed value, and cannot be calculated when open-end class intervals are present.
facts.locator: Printed p. 50, Merits and Demerits of Arithmetic Mean

facts.statement: The geometric mean of n positive values is the nth root of their product, taking account of compounding from period to period; for grouped data each value is raised to its frequency and the root is of the total frequency. It is used for index numbers, annual return on a portfolio and compounded annual growth rates, and is not much affected by sampling fluctuations. It cannot be calculated when any value is zero or negative, and is harder to compute and understand.

The harmonic mean is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals of the observations: n divided by the sum of 1/x (for grouped data n divided by the sum of f/x). It is appropriate for averaging ratios or rates whose values are measured in different units, such as speed (km per hour) and different rates in finance, whereas the arithmetic mean suits values with the same units.

For two numbers, arithmetic mean x harmonic mean = (geometric mean) squared; the courseware states the ordering as AM > HM > GM and uses the relation to find an HM from an AM of 16 and a GM of 8 (its final division is printed as 64/6 although the quotient is 64/16 = 4). For positive values that are not all equal the standard ordering is AM > GM > HM.
facts.locator: Printed p. 53, Comparison and Example 14 (ordering and arithmetic in the courseware differ from the standard result)

facts.statement: The median is the middle value when the observations are arranged in order: for an odd number n it is the ((n+1)/2)th observation and for an even number it is the average of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th. For grouped data the median class is the class whose less-than cumulative frequency first exceeds N/2, and median = l1 + ((N/2 - cf) / f) x (l2 - l1), where l1 and l2 are the limits of the median class, f its frequency and cf the cumulative frequency of the class before it. For a discrete frequency table the median is the value whose cumulative frequency first exceeds N/2. Inclusive classes are first converted to class boundaries.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 53-57, section 3.6 and Examples 15 to 19

facts.statement: Quartiles divide an ordered distribution into four equal parts: Q1 (lower quartile), Q2 (the median) and Q3 (upper quartile). For grouped data they use the same interpolation as the median, with N/4, N/2 and 3N/4 in place of N/2. The median is rigidly defined and not affected by extreme values, but it is not based on all observations, is affected by sampling fluctuations and does not lend itself to further algebraic treatment.

The mode is the most frequently occurring value; a distribution can have two or more modes (multimodal). For grouped data the modal class is the class of highest frequency and mode = l1 + ((f1 - f0) / (2 f1 - f0 - f2)) x (l2 - l1), with f1 the modal class frequency and f0 and f2 the frequencies of the classes before and after it. The mode is easy to understand and little affected by sampling fluctuations, but is ill-defined, not based on all observations and not amenable to algebraic treatment. For moderately skewed data the three measures are related by Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 59-61, section 3.7 and Examples 22 to 24

facts.statement: Dispersion measures the scatter of items about the averages. The absolute measures are range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation; the corresponding relative measures are the coefficients of range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and variation. A good measure is rigidly defined, based on all observations, simple, capable of further algebraic treatment and little affected by sampling fluctuations.

The range is maximum minus minimum and the coefficient of range is (max - min) / (max + min). The range is easy to understand and calculate but is not based on all observations, has no sampling stability, and becomes less satisfactory as the amount of data grows.

Quartile deviation is the half of the interquartile range, QD = (Q3 - Q1) / 2, and its coefficient is (Q3 - Q1) / (Q3 + Q1). It is easy to calculate and not affected by extreme values, but it is not based on all observations, not capable of algebraic treatment and affected by sampling fluctuations.

Mean deviation is the arithmetic mean of the absolute deviations from an average: Sum|x - mean| / n for raw data and Sum f|x - mean| / Sum f for grouped data, with the class marks as x; the coefficient of mean deviation is the mean deviation divided by the average used. Mean deviation is smallest when taken about the median. It is based on all observations and easy to calculate, but ignores signs and so is not capable of further algebraic treatment.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 63-65, Mean Deviation and Examples 26 to 28

facts.statement: Standard deviation is the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean: sigma = sqrt(Sum(x - mean)^2 / n) = sqrt(Sum x^2 / n - mean^2) for raw data, and sqrt(Sum f x^2 / N - (Sum f x / N)^2) for grouped data. The coefficient of variation is CV = (sigma / mean) x 100 per cent. A small standard deviation means a high degree of consistency and homogeneity. The measure is rigidly defined and based on all observations, but it is not easy to compute or understand and gives more weight to extreme items.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 65-67, section 3.11 and Examples 29 to 31

facts.statement: Skewness is the degree of departure from a symmetrical distribution. In positive skew the longer tail is on the right and the mean and median are greater than the mode; in negative skew the longer tail is on the left and the mean and median are less than the mode. Karl Pearson's measure is beta1 = mu3^2 / mu2^3, where mu2 and mu3 are the second and third central moments (the averages of (x - mean)^2 and (x - mean)^3, weighted by frequency for grouped data); the direction of skew follows the sign of mu3.

Kurtosis describes the peakedness or flatness of a distribution and the weight of its tails. A distribution with the peak of the normal curve is mesokurtic, a higher and sharper peak with fatter tails is leptokurtic, and a lower, flatter peak with thinner tails is platykurtic. The measure is beta2 = mu4 / mu2^2, with mu4 the fourth central moment; the courseware compares it with 0 (the usual comparison value for the normal distribution in this form is 3) and prints "mesokurtic" twice in its list of cases, and its worked example computes beta2 = 0.025 from 3,600,000 / 12,000^2 where the central moments are divided by n (mu4 = 36,000 and mu2 = 120 give 2.5).
facts.locator: Printed pp. 68-69, section 3.12 and Example 32 (convention and arithmetic in the courseware differ from the standard result)

payload.title: What an average is for, and what makes one good
payload.core_explanation_md:
A long list of numbers is hard to hold in the mind. An **average** squeezes it into one representative value, and lets you compare one group with another. There are three families:

| Average | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Mean (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic) | A calculated value from all the data |
| Median | The middle value of the ordered data |
| Mode | The most frequent value |

A good average is clearly defined, simple, uses every observation, can be used in further algebra, is stable between samples, is not dominated by extreme values and is easy to interpret. No single average ticks every box, so choosing one means deciding which property matters for the question at hand.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This is why you will see the median for incomes (extreme values do not dominate), the mean for totals that must add up, and the mode for "what is the most common outcome".

self_check.prompt_text: Name two properties of a good average, and say which average gives up the property of using every observation.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: rigidly defined, simple, uses all observations, algebraic treatment, stable under sampling, not unduly affected by extremes, easy to interpret. The median and the mode do not use every observation.

payload.title: Arithmetic mean: raw, grouped, combined and corrected
payload.core_explanation_md:
One idea, four situations:

- **Raw data**: add the values and divide by how many there are.
- **Grouped data**: multiply each value (or class mark) by its frequency, add, and divide by the total frequency.
- **Combined mean**: you cannot just average two group means; weight each by its group size.
- **Corrected mean**: if one value was recorded wrongly, rebuild the total (mean times n), take out the wrong value, put in the right one, and divide again.

A missing value or frequency is found by writing the mean as an equation and solving for the unknown.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The corrected-mean method is the same as adjusting a ledger total: you do not recount everything, you reverse the error. Combined means appear whenever branches, products or customer segments are pooled.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n},\quad \bar{x} = \frac{\sum f x}{\sum f},\quad \bar{x}_c = \frac{n_1 \bar{x}_1 + n_2 \bar{x}_2}{n_1 + n_2}

variables.name: Observation, or class mark for grouped data
Means of the groups being pooled

assumptions: For grouped data the class mark stands for every value in the class, so the grouped mean is an approximation.
The corrected mean uses the same n as the original.
common_errors: Averaging two group means without weighting by group size.
Using the class limit instead of the class mark for grouped data.
Correcting the mean directly instead of correcting the sum.

self_check.prompt_text: A mean of 50 observations is 40. One value recorded as 90 should have been 60. What is the corrected mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Original sum 2,000; corrected sum 2,000 - 90 + 60 = 1,970; corrected mean 1,970/50 = 39.4.

payload.title: When the arithmetic mean misleads
payload.core_explanation_md:
The mean is the workhorse: it uses every observation, is easy to compute and supports further algebra. Its strength is also its weakness, because every value pulls on it.

- **Extreme values** drag it. One very large loan moves the average loan.
- **Skewed data**: it sits away from where most observations lie.
- **Open-end classes** such as "above 50 lakh" have no class mark, so the mean cannot be computed properly.
- **Ratios and percentages**: averaging rates with the arithmetic mean can give a wrong answer.
- It may equal no actual value (an average of 2.4 children).

When these problems bite, look to the median, or to the geometric or harmonic mean for rates.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A useful test is to compare the mean with the median: if they are far apart, a few extreme observations are probably doing the work.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the arithmetic mean a poor choice for a table whose last class is "above 50 lakh"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The open-end class has no upper limit, so it has no class mark to multiply by its frequency, and the mean cannot be computed accurately.

payload.title: Geometric and harmonic means, and how they compare with the arithmetic mean
payload.core_explanation_md:
Use the right mean for the kind of quantity:

| Mean | Formula idea | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arithmetic | Sum divided by n | Values in the same units |
| Geometric | nth root of the product | Growth that compounds: average annual growth, index numbers, portfolio return |
| Harmonic | n divided by the sum of reciprocals | Rates and ratios in different units, such as speed |

Geometric needs all values positive. For positive values that are not all equal, **AM is larger than GM, which is larger than HM**. For exactly two numbers, AM x HM = GM squared.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Why the geometric mean for growth? Growth factors multiply, so the single constant factor that gives the same overall result is their geometric mean, not their arithmetic mean. The courseware prints the order as AM > HM > GM; the standard result, which the worked examples here confirm, puts GM above HM.

formula_spec.latex_expression: GM = \left(x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n\right)^{1/n},\quad HM = \frac{n}{\sum 1/x_i},\quad AM \times HM = GM^2 \text{ (two numbers)}

variables.name: Positive observations (growth factors for GM, rates for HM)

assumptions: All values positive for GM and HM.
For HM to be the right average of speeds, the distances travelled at each speed must be equal.
AM x HM = GM squared holds only for two values.
common_errors: Using the arithmetic mean of growth rates to describe compounded growth.
Taking the harmonic mean when different distances are covered at different speeds without weighting.
Applying AM x HM = GM squared to more than two numbers.

self_check.prompt_text: An account grows by factors 1.20 and 1.05 over two years. Which mean of the two factors gives the constant yearly factor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The geometric mean, the square root of 1.20 x 1.05 = 1.26, which is about 1.1225.

payload.title: Median and quartiles, raw and grouped
payload.core_explanation_md:
Sort first. Then:

- **Raw data**: with an odd count take the middle value; with an even count average the two middle values.
- **Grouped data**: find the **median class**, the first class whose less-than cumulative frequency goes beyond N/2, then interpolate inside it.
- **Quartiles** work the same way with N/4 (Q1), N/2 (Q2, the median) and 3N/4 (Q3).

In each case the interpolation starts at the lower limit of the class, adds the fraction of the class still needed and scales by the class width. Make sure the classes are continuous (use boundaries for inclusive classes) before you start.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The median is the safe choice when extreme values or open-end classes are present, because it needs only the order, not the size, of the outer values.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{Median} = l_1 + \frac{N/2 - cf}{f}\,(l_2 - l_1),\quad Q_1:\ N/4,\quad Q_3:\ 3N/4

variables.name: Lower and upper limits of the median (or quartile) class
Cumulative frequency of the class before it

assumptions: Classes are continuous, in ascending order.
The median class is the one whose cumulative frequency first exceeds N/2 (N/4 or 3N/4 for quartiles).
common_errors: Using the class frequency instead of the preceding cumulative frequency for cf.
Forgetting the class width factor.
Using N/2 for every quartile.

self_check.prompt_text: N = 80 and the cumulative frequencies of the first three classes are 10, 30 and 55. Which class holds the median, and which holds Q1?
self_check.expected_takeaway: N/2 = 40, first exceeded by 55, so the third class; N/4 = 20, first exceeded by 30, so the second class.

payload.title: Mode, and the mean-median-mode relation
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **mode** is the value that occurs most often. In a frequency table, the **modal class** is the class with the highest frequency. The mode is then placed inside it by pulling it towards the more crowded neighbour: if the class after the modal class is fuller than the one before, the mode sits above the middle of the modal class.

A distribution can have two modes (bimodal) or more (multimodal).

For moderately skewed data the three averages are tied together: **Mode = 3 x Median - 2 x Mean**. If two are known, estimate the third.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The relation is an empirical rule, not an identity. It works well for single-peaked, only mildly skewed distributions and poorly for very uneven ones.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{Mode} = l_1 + \frac{f_1 - f_0}{2 f_1 - f_0 - f_2}\,(l_2 - l_1),\qquad \text{Mode} \approx 3\,\text{Median} - 2\,\text{Mean}

variables.name: Frequencies of the classes before and after it

assumptions: Equal class widths.
The relation with the median and mean holds only approximately, for moderately skewed single-peaked data.
common_errors: Taking the middle of the modal class without adjusting for the neighbours.
Swapping f0 and f2.
Treating the three-median-two-mean relation as exact.

self_check.prompt_text: Modal class 20-30 has frequency 30, the class before has 20 and the class after has 10. Is the mode above or below the middle (25) of the class?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Below: the class before is fuller than the one after, which pulls the mode down. 20 + (30 - 20) / (60 - 20 - 10) x 10 = 23.33.

payload.title: Choosing between mean, median and mode
payload.core_explanation_md:
Pick the average that matches the question and the shape of the data.

| Average | Best when | Weak when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arithmetic mean | Totals matter; data roughly symmetric | Extreme values, skew, open-end classes |
| Median | Skewed data, extreme values, open ends | You need further algebra, or every value must count |
| Mode | You want the most common value | The distribution has no clear peak or several |
| Geometric mean | Compounded growth | Zero or negative values |
| Harmonic mean | Rates over equal distances or equal amounts | Zero values |

If the data are **positively skewed**, expect mean > median > mode; if **negatively skewed**, the reverse.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: When in doubt, report the mean and the median together. A large gap between them tells the reader the data are skewed.

self_check.prompt_text: Deposit balances are strongly right-skewed. Which of mean and median will be larger, and which would you quote as "typical"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The mean will be larger; the median is the better typical value because large balances do not drag it.

payload.title: Dispersion: how spread out the data are
payload.core_explanation_md:
Two sets of branch deposits can have the same average and be very different: one steady, one swinging wildly. An average hides that. **Dispersion** measures the scatter.

| Absolute (in the units of the data) | Relative (a pure number, for comparison) |
| --- | --- |
| Range | Coefficient of range |
| Quartile deviation | Coefficient of quartile deviation |
| Mean deviation | Coefficient of mean deviation |
| Standard deviation | Coefficient of variation |

Use an **absolute** measure within one series. Use a **relative** one to compare series measured in different units or with very different averages.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: As with averages, a good measure is well defined, uses all observations, is simple, allows algebra and is stable between samples. The standard deviation does best on most of these, which is why it is the standard.

self_check.prompt_text: You want to compare the spread of loan amounts (in rupees) with the spread of loan tenures (in months). Absolute or relative measure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Relative, because the units differ; use the coefficient of variation.

payload.title: Range, quartile deviation and mean deviation
payload.core_explanation_md:
Three ways to measure scatter, from rough to thorough:

- **Range**: largest minus smallest. Quick, but uses only two observations.
- **Quartile deviation**: half the gap between the upper and lower quartiles. It ignores the extremes, so it is steady.
- **Mean deviation**: the average of the absolute distances from an average (the mean, or the median, which gives the smaller value). It uses every observation, but throwing away the signs makes it awkward for further algebra.

Each has a coefficient that divides by a comparable quantity, so you can compare series.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Remember what each coefficient divides by: the sum of the extremes for range, the sum of the quartiles for quartile deviation, and the average used for mean deviation.

formula_spec.latex_expression: R = x_{max} - x_{min},\quad QD = \frac{Q_3 - Q_1}{2},\quad MD = \frac{\sum f |x - \bar{x}|}{\sum f}

variables.name: Range: (max - min)/(max + min); QD: (Q3 - Q1)/(Q3 + Q1); MD: MD divided by the mean

assumptions: Absolute deviations are used in MD (signs ignored).
Class marks stand for the values in a grouped table.
common_errors: Dividing the range by the mean instead of by max + min for the coefficient.
Forgetting to take absolute values in MD.
Using Q3 - Q1 without halving for QD.

self_check.prompt_text: Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 28. What are the quartile deviation and its coefficient?

payload.title: Standard deviation, variance and coefficient of variation
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **standard deviation** squares each deviation from the mean (so the signs cannot cancel), averages the squares, and takes the root to get back to the original units. The average of the squares is the **variance**.

A shortcut avoids computing every deviation: **mean of the squares minus square of the mean**.

The **coefficient of variation** expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, which makes different series comparable. The series with the smaller CV is the more consistent.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This unit divides by n (the whole data set is treated as the population). Later, when estimating from a sample, a different divisor is used; check which the question intends.

assumptions: Divisor is N, not N - 1.
The mean is not zero when CV is used.
common_errors: Squaring each frequency-weighted total instead of squaring the mean (mean of squares less square of the mean).
Taking the root before dividing by N.
Reporting the variance when the standard deviation is asked.

self_check.prompt_text: Mean 60 and standard deviation 9. What is the CV, and what does a smaller CV in another branch tell you?
self_check.expected_takeaway: CV = 9/60 x 100 = 15 per cent; the branch with the smaller CV is more consistent.

payload.title: Reading a standard deviation and comparing consistency
payload.core_explanation_md:
A standard deviation by itself needs a yardstick. Is 20 big? For deposits averaging 80 it is large; for 200 it is modest. That is the job of the **coefficient of variation**.

| Branch | Mean daily transactions | Standard deviation | CV |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 200 | 30 | 15 per cent |
| B | 80 | 20 | 25 per cent |

Branch B has the smaller standard deviation but the larger CV, so its volumes swing more *relative to its size*. Branch A is the more consistent. Quoting the standard deviation alone would have given the opposite impression.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The standard deviation gives more weight to extreme items (squaring magnifies large deviations), so a few outliers can inflate it. Always look at the data behind the number.

self_check.prompt_text: Two series have the same mean. The first has standard deviation 12 and the second 8. Which is more consistent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The second: with equal means the smaller standard deviation also means the smaller CV.

payload.title: Skewness and kurtosis: shape beyond average and spread
payload.core_explanation_md:
Two distributions can share a mean and a standard deviation and still look different.

**Skewness** is lopsidedness.

| Skew | Longer tail | Order of the averages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive | Right | Mean > median > mode |
| Symmetric | Neither | All equal |
| Negative | Left | Mean < median < mode |

It is measured with the **third central moment** (the average cube of deviations from the mean): positive means a longer right tail, negative a longer left tail, zero a symmetric shape.

**Kurtosis** is peakedness and tail weight, measured from the fourth central moment as mu4 divided by mu2 squared. Taller and sharper with fat tails is **leptokurtic**; like the normal curve is **mesokurtic**; flatter with thin tails is **platykurtic**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A caution on conventions. In this form, mu4/mu2 squared equals 3 for the normal curve, so leptokurtic means above 3. The courseware compares the value with 0 (the "excess" form, measured as mu4/mu2 squared minus 3). Check which form a question uses.

self_check.prompt_text: Mean 52, median 48, mode 44. Is the skew positive or negative, and which tail is longer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Positive skew (mean > median > mode); the longer tail is on the right.

payload.title: Pooling three staff groups, then correcting one salary
payload.core_explanation_md: A bank has 40 clerks with a mean monthly pay of Rs 32,000, 25 officers with a mean of Rs 54,000 and 15 managers with a mean of Rs 80,000. Find the combined mean. Later it is found that one manager's pay was entered as Rs 80,000 when it should have been Rs 98,000. Find the corrected mean.

worked_steps.description: Total pay of each group (size x mean).
Total pay of all groups and number of staff.
Correct the total: remove the wrong value, add the right one.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Combined mean Rs 47,875 per month; corrected mean Rs 48,100 per month

self_check.prompt_text: The plain average of the three group means is Rs 55,333. Why is it wrong?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It ignores group sizes: there are many more clerks than managers, so the clerks' lower pay should weigh more.

payload.title: Finding a missing frequency from a known mean
payload.core_explanation_md: Loan sizes (Rs lakh) are grouped: 0-10 has 8 loans, 10-20 has 12, 20-30 has an unknown number x, and 30-40 has 10. The mean loan size is Rs 22 lakh. Find x.

worked_steps.description: Sum of frequency x mark in terms of x.

self_check.prompt_text: What would the mean be if x were 0?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 570/30 = 19 lakh, lower because there are no loans in the higher-value class.

payload.title: Average growth and average speed: geometric and harmonic means
payload.core_explanation_md: Part A: a branch's deposits grew by 0 per cent, 10 per cent and 21 per cent in three successive years. What constant yearly growth gives the same result? Part B: an officer drives the same distance to a branch at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. What is the average speed for the round trip? Check AM x HM = GM squared on the two speeds.

worked_steps.intermediate_result: multiply to give the overall growth
1.10, a constant 10 per cent a year

worked_steps.description: A: the arithmetic mean of the rates overstates it.
B: equal distances, so use the harmonic mean.
B: AM x HM = GM squared.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Constant growth 10 per cent a year (not 10.33); average speed 48 km/h

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the average speed 48 and not the arithmetic mean 50?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The officer spends more time at the slower speed, because the same distance takes longer at 40 km/h; the harmonic mean accounts for that.

payload.title: Median and both quartiles of 120 loan sizes
payload.core_explanation_md: Loan sizes (Rs lakh) of 120 accounts: 0-5 has 12, 5-10 has 20, 10-15 has 40, 15-20 has 36 and 20-25 has 12. Find the median, Q1 and Q3.

worked_steps.description: Median: N/2 = 60. First cumulative frequency above 60 is 72, class 10-15 (cf before = 32).
Q1: N/4 = 30. First cumulative frequency above 30 is 32, class 5-10 (cf before = 12).
Q3: 3N/4 = 90. First cumulative frequency above 90 is 108, class 15-20 (cf before = 72).

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Median Rs 13.5 lakh; Q1 Rs 9.5 lakh; Q3 Rs 17.5 lakh

self_check.prompt_text: Half of the loans are below which value, and what share lie between Q1 and Q3?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Half are below Rs 13.5 lakh; half of all loans (the middle 50 per cent) lie between Rs 9.5 and Rs 17.5 lakh.

payload.title: Mode of the same loans, checked against the mean and median
payload.core_explanation_md: Using the same 120 loan sizes (classes 0-5 to 20-25 with frequencies 12, 20, 40, 36, 12; median 13.5), find the mode from the grouped formula, and test the relation Mode = 3 Median - 2 Mean.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: Mode Rs 14.17 lakh; it agrees with 3 x median - 2 x mean (also 14.17), which holds here because the distribution is only mildly skewed

self_check.prompt_text: Here mean 13.17 < median 13.5 < mode 14.17. What does that order say about the skew?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Negative skew: the mean and the median are below the mode, with a longer left tail.

payload.title: Quartile deviation and mean deviation of the loan data
payload.core_explanation_md: For the 120 loans (classes 0-5 to 20-25, frequencies 12, 20, 40, 36, 12; Q1 = 9.5, Q3 = 17.5; mean 13.1667 lakh), find the quartile deviation, its coefficient, the mean deviation about the mean and its coefficient.

worked_steps.description: Absolute deviations of the class marks from 13.1667.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: QD Rs 4.0 lakh, coefficient 0.2963; mean deviation Rs 4.47 lakh, coefficient 0.3392

self_check.prompt_text: Why can the coefficients be compared with those of a series measured in another unit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Each coefficient divides a deviation by a quantity in the same unit, so the unit cancels and a pure number remains.

payload.title: Standard deviation, variance and CV of the loan data; two branches compared
payload.core_explanation_md: For the 120 loans (marks 2.5, 7.5, 12.5, 17.5, 22.5 with frequencies 12, 20, 40, 36, 12), find the variance, standard deviation and coefficient of variation. Then compare two branches: A has mean 200 and standard deviation 30, B has mean 80 and standard deviation 20.

items.title: What an average is for, and what makes one good
items.core_explanation_md:
A long list of numbers is hard to hold in the mind. An **average** squeezes it into one representative value, and lets you compare one group with another. There are three families:

| Average | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Mean (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic) | A calculated value from all the data |
| Median | The middle value of the ordered data |
| Mode | The most frequent value |

A good average is clearly defined, simple, uses every observation, can be used in further algebra, is stable between samples, is not dominated by extreme values and is easy to interpret. No single average ticks every box, so choosing one means deciding which property matters for the question at hand.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is why you will see the median for incomes (extreme values do not dominate), the mean for totals that must add up, and the mode for "what is the most common outcome".

self_check.prompt_text: Name two properties of a good average, and say which average gives up the property of using every observation.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: rigidly defined, simple, uses all observations, algebraic treatment, stable under sampling, not unduly affected by extremes, easy to interpret. The median and the mode do not use every observation.

items.title: Arithmetic mean: raw, grouped, combined and corrected
items.core_explanation_md:
One idea, four situations:

- **Raw data**: add the values and divide by how many there are.
- **Grouped data**: multiply each value (or class mark) by its frequency, add, and divide by the total frequency.
- **Combined mean**: you cannot just average two group means; weight each by its group size.
- **Corrected mean**: if one value was recorded wrongly, rebuild the total (mean times n), take out the wrong value, put in the right one, and divide again.

A missing value or frequency is found by writing the mean as an equation and solving for the unknown.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The corrected-mean method is the same as adjusting a ledger total: you do not recount everything, you reverse the error. Combined means appear whenever branches, products or customer segments are pooled.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n},\quad \bar{x} = \frac{\sum f x}{\sum f},\quad \bar{x}_c = \frac{n_1 \bar{x}_1 + n_2 \bar{x}_2}{n_1 + n_2}

variables.name: Observation, or class mark for grouped data
Means of the groups being pooled

assumptions: For grouped data the class mark stands for every value in the class, so the grouped mean is an approximation.
The corrected mean uses the same n as the original.
common_errors: Averaging two group means without weighting by group size.
Using the class limit instead of the class mark for grouped data.
Correcting the mean directly instead of correcting the sum.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Original sum 2,000; corrected sum 2,000 - 90 + 60 = 1,970; corrected mean 1,970/50 = 39.4.

items.title: When the arithmetic mean misleads
items.core_explanation_md:
The mean is the workhorse: it uses every observation, is easy to compute and supports further algebra. Its strength is also its weakness, because every value pulls on it.

- **Extreme values** drag it. One very large loan moves the average loan.
- **Skewed data**: it sits away from where most observations lie.
- **Open-end classes** such as "above 50 lakh" have no class mark, so the mean cannot be computed properly.
- **Ratios and percentages**: averaging rates with the arithmetic mean can give a wrong answer.
- It may equal no actual value (an average of 2.4 children).

When these problems bite, look to the median, or to the geometric or harmonic mean for rates.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A useful test is to compare the mean with the median: if they are far apart, a few extreme observations are probably doing the work.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The open-end class has no upper limit, so it has no class mark to multiply by its frequency, and the mean cannot be computed accurately.

items.title: Geometric and harmonic means, and how they compare with the arithmetic mean
items.core_explanation_md:
Use the right mean for the kind of quantity:

| Mean | Formula idea | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arithmetic | Sum divided by n | Values in the same units |
| Geometric | nth root of the product | Growth that compounds: average annual growth, index numbers, portfolio return |
| Harmonic | n divided by the sum of reciprocals | Rates and ratios in different units, such as speed |

Geometric needs all values positive. For positive values that are not all equal, **AM is larger than GM, which is larger than HM**. For exactly two numbers, AM x HM = GM squared.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why the geometric mean for growth? Growth factors multiply, so the single constant factor that gives the same overall result is their geometric mean, not their arithmetic mean. The courseware prints the order as AM > HM > GM; the standard result, which the worked examples here confirm, puts GM above HM.

formula_spec.latex_expression: GM = \left(x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n\right)^{1/n},\quad HM = \frac{n}{\sum 1/x_i},\quad AM \times HM = GM^2 \text{ (two numbers)}

variables.name: Positive observations (growth factors for GM, rates for HM)

assumptions: All values positive for GM and HM.
For HM to be the right average of speeds, the distances travelled at each speed must be equal.
AM x HM = GM squared holds only for two values.
common_errors: Using the arithmetic mean of growth rates to describe compounded growth.
Taking the harmonic mean when different distances are covered at different speeds without weighting.
Applying AM x HM = GM squared to more than two numbers.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The geometric mean, the square root of 1.20 x 1.05 = 1.26, which is about 1.1225.

items.title: Median and quartiles, raw and grouped
items.core_explanation_md:
Sort first. Then:

- **Raw data**: with an odd count take the middle value; with an even count average the two middle values.
- **Grouped data**: find the **median class**, the first class whose less-than cumulative frequency goes beyond N/2, then interpolate inside it.
- **Quartiles** work the same way with N/4 (Q1), N/2 (Q2, the median) and 3N/4 (Q3).

In each case the interpolation starts at the lower limit of the class, adds the fraction of the class still needed and scales by the class width. Make sure the classes are continuous (use boundaries for inclusive classes) before you start.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The median is the safe choice when extreme values or open-end classes are present, because it needs only the order, not the size, of the outer values.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{Median} = l_1 + \frac{N/2 - cf}{f}\,(l_2 - l_1),\quad Q_1:\ N/4,\quad Q_3:\ 3N/4

variables.name: Lower and upper limits of the median (or quartile) class
Cumulative frequency of the class before it

assumptions: Classes are continuous, in ascending order.
The median class is the one whose cumulative frequency first exceeds N/2 (N/4 or 3N/4 for quartiles).
common_errors: Using the class frequency instead of the preceding cumulative frequency for cf.
Forgetting the class width factor.
Using N/2 for every quartile.

items.title: Mode, and the mean-median-mode relation
items.core_explanation_md:
The **mode** is the value that occurs most often. In a frequency table, the **modal class** is the class with the highest frequency. The mode is then placed inside it by pulling it towards the more crowded neighbour: if the class after the modal class is fuller than the one before, the mode sits above the middle of the modal class.

A distribution can have two modes (bimodal) or more (multimodal).

For moderately skewed data the three averages are tied together: **Mode = 3 x Median - 2 x Mean**. If two are known, estimate the third.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The relation is an empirical rule, not an identity. It works well for single-peaked, only mildly skewed distributions and poorly for very uneven ones.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{Mode} = l_1 + \frac{f_1 - f_0}{2 f_1 - f_0 - f_2}\,(l_2 - l_1),\qquad \text{Mode} \approx 3\,\text{Median} - 2\,\text{Mean}

variables.name: Frequencies of the classes before and after it

assumptions: Equal class widths.
The relation with the median and mean holds only approximately, for moderately skewed single-peaked data.
common_errors: Taking the middle of the modal class without adjusting for the neighbours.
Swapping f0 and f2.
Treating the three-median-two-mean relation as exact.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Below: the class before is fuller than the one after, which pulls the mode down. 20 + (30 - 20) / (60 - 20 - 10) x 10 = 23.33.

items.title: Choosing between mean, median and mode
items.core_explanation_md:
Pick the average that matches the question and the shape of the data.

| Average | Best when | Weak when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arithmetic mean | Totals matter; data roughly symmetric | Extreme values, skew, open-end classes |
| Median | Skewed data, extreme values, open ends | You need further algebra, or every value must count |
| Mode | You want the most common value | The distribution has no clear peak or several |
| Geometric mean | Compounded growth | Zero or negative values |
| Harmonic mean | Rates over equal distances or equal amounts | Zero values |

items.title: Dispersion: how spread out the data are
items.core_explanation_md:
Two sets of branch deposits can have the same average and be very different: one steady, one swinging wildly. An average hides that. **Dispersion** measures the scatter.

| Absolute (in the units of the data) | Relative (a pure number, for comparison) |
| --- | --- |
| Range | Coefficient of range |
| Quartile deviation | Coefficient of quartile deviation |
| Mean deviation | Coefficient of mean deviation |
| Standard deviation | Coefficient of variation |

Use an **absolute** measure within one series. Use a **relative** one to compare series measured in different units or with very different averages.
items.expanded_explanation_md: As with averages, a good measure is well defined, uses all observations, is simple, allows algebra and is stable between samples. The standard deviation does best on most of these, which is why it is the standard.

self_check.prompt_text: You want to compare the spread of loan amounts (in rupees) with the spread of loan tenures (in months). Absolute or relative measure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Relative, because the units differ; use the coefficient of variation.

items.title: Range, quartile deviation and mean deviation
items.core_explanation_md:
Three ways to measure scatter, from rough to thorough:

- **Range**: largest minus smallest. Quick, but uses only two observations.
- **Quartile deviation**: half the gap between the upper and lower quartiles. It ignores the extremes, so it is steady.
- **Mean deviation**: the average of the absolute distances from an average (the mean, or the median, which gives the smaller value). It uses every observation, but throwing away the signs makes it awkward for further algebra.

Each has a coefficient that divides by a comparable quantity, so you can compare series.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Remember what each coefficient divides by: the sum of the extremes for range, the sum of the quartiles for quartile deviation, and the average used for mean deviation.

items.title: Standard deviation, variance and coefficient of variation
items.core_explanation_md:
The **standard deviation** squares each deviation from the mean (so the signs cannot cancel), averages the squares, and takes the root to get back to the original units. The average of the squares is the **variance**.

A shortcut avoids computing every deviation: **mean of the squares minus square of the mean**.

The **coefficient of variation** expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, which makes different series comparable. The series with the smaller CV is the more consistent.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This unit divides by n (the whole data set is treated as the population). Later, when estimating from a sample, a different divisor is used; check which the question intends.

assumptions: Divisor is N, not N - 1.
The mean is not zero when CV is used.
common_errors: Squaring each frequency-weighted total instead of squaring the mean (mean of squares less square of the mean).
Taking the root before dividing by N.
Reporting the variance when the standard deviation is asked.

self_check.prompt_text: Mean 60 and standard deviation 9. What is the CV, and what does a smaller CV in another branch tell you?
self_check.expected_takeaway: CV = 9/60 x 100 = 15 per cent; the branch with the smaller CV is more consistent.

items.title: Reading a standard deviation and comparing consistency
items.core_explanation_md:
A standard deviation by itself needs a yardstick. Is 20 big? For deposits averaging 80 it is large; for 200 it is modest. That is the job of the **coefficient of variation**.

| Branch | Mean daily transactions | Standard deviation | CV |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 200 | 30 | 15 per cent |
| B | 80 | 20 | 25 per cent |

items.title: Skewness and kurtosis: shape beyond average and spread
items.core_explanation_md:
Two distributions can share a mean and a standard deviation and still look different.

**Skewness** is lopsidedness.

| Skew | Longer tail | Order of the averages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive | Right | Mean > median > mode |
| Symmetric | Neither | All equal |
| Negative | Left | Mean < median < mode |

It is measured with the **third central moment** (the average cube of deviations from the mean): positive means a longer right tail, negative a longer left tail, zero a symmetric shape.

**Kurtosis** is peakedness and tail weight, measured from the fourth central moment as mu4 divided by mu2 squared. Taller and sharper with fat tails is **leptokurtic**; like the normal curve is **mesokurtic**; flatter with thin tails is **platykurtic**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A caution on conventions. In this form, mu4/mu2 squared equals 3 for the normal curve, so leptokurtic means above 3. The courseware compares the value with 0 (the "excess" form, measured as mu4/mu2 squared minus 3). Check which form a question uses.

self_check.prompt_text: Mean 52, median 48, mode 44. Is the skew positive or negative, and which tail is longer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Positive skew (mean > median > mode); the longer tail is on the right.

items.stem_md: To compare the spread of loan amounts (in rupees) with the spread of loan tenures (in months), which measure should you use?

options.text_md: The range of each
options.explanation_md: Ranges are in different units and cannot be compared.

options.text_md: The standard deviation of each
options.explanation_md: Standard deviations are also in different units.

options.text_md: A coefficient such as the coefficient of variation
options.explanation_md: Relative measures are pure numbers and allow comparison across units.

options.text_md: The mean of each
options.explanation_md: The mean describes the centre, not the spread.

items.correct_explanation_md: Relative measures of dispersion (the coefficients) are free of units and so can be compared across series.

items.stem_md: The main weakness of the range as a measure of dispersion is that

options.text_md: It is based only on the two extreme observations
options.explanation_md: The range ignores all values between the largest and the smallest.

options.text_md: It is hard to calculate
options.explanation_md: It is the simplest measure.

options.text_md: It cannot be computed for positive numbers
options.explanation_md: It can be computed for any set of numbers.

options.text_md: It is always zero
options.explanation_md: It is zero only if all observations are equal.

options.text_md: Q is less consistent, because its CV (20 per cent) is higher than P's (15 per cent)

items.correct_explanation_md: Consistency is judged by the coefficient of variation: the smaller the CV, the more consistent. P is at 15 per cent and Q at 20 per cent.
